newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ seen risking trouble with compulsory pensions.
newsitem.headline: NZ seen risking trouble with compulsory pensions.

text.p: New Zealand's new centre-right coalition government is risking its thin parliamentary majority over the controversial issue of compulsory retirement savings, analysts said on Thursday.
Its plans to put a compulsory pension scheme, known as 'compulsory super', to a September referendum are drawing flak from many quarters, including from within its own ranks.
"The short answer is they are risking trouble," said Auckland University political science lecturer Raymond Miller.
"The coalition government is potentially going to be in a fairly embarrassing position after the referendum."

The National-New Zealand First, two-party coalition is plagued by debate not only on the merits of compulsory versus voluntary retirement savings, but also by the mechanics of organising a credible referendum in a short space of time on a scheme for which final details have yet to be released.
Treasurer and NZ First leader Winston Peters said on Wednesday design work was "far from finalised" but he wanted the scheme made public in early July.
NZ First has outlined a scheme that would eventually divert about eight percent of income into pension savings and suggested that this requirement could be offset by compensatory tax cuts.
Peters has radically shifted on parts of the initial plan, however, dropping a government guarantee on returns, for example. Critics say he is revamping the whole pension system.
Opposition parties Labour and the Alliance have called for the referendum to be postponed, saying the public will know details of the scheme for only around eight weeks before voting.
The government's pledge to back compulsory pensions if they are approved by a simple majority of those voting -- irrespective of voter turnout -- is also coming under fire.
Some opposition parties have said they would attack the credibility of any result that is not clear-cut.
"What credibility would it have if there was a 30 percent turnout and only 17 percent -- just over half -- opted for it?" asked Alliance leader Jim Anderton.
Even in National's ranks a group of backbenchers have asked the same question, and made a clear threat to vote against the legislation.

"If there is a turnout under 50 percent, I will consider it is not a mandate from the public," Waipareira MP Brian Neeson told Reuters. He said more than half the National caucus felt as he did, but would not guess how many might cross the floor.
The government has 61 seats in the 120-member single-chamber parliament.
A cross-party group of women MPs has also been established to oppose compulsory savings, which they see as discriminatory.
Miller said cross-party cooperation should set alarm bells ringing for the government.

"Quite clearly the National caucus is divided on the issue, and that provides potential for real embarrassment for National. Particularly so for the prime minister, who has publicly endorsed the compulsory superannuation idea," he said.
Prime Minister and National Party leader Jim Bolger this week foreshadowed higher taxes or a cut in the State pension if compulsory superannuation did not win public support.
"The inevitability is we are going to have about a doubling of the number of retired New Zealanders in the future and it is clearly going to cost more for retirement income," Bolger said.
"We either prepare for that in savings or look to the increase of taxes or the reducing of benefits in the future."
